title: The Mystery of the Missing Whistle Lever
markdown:
Volunteer Morning at the Otterton Railway Museum smelled of coal smoke, polishing wax, and journeys long past. The grand echoing halls held a peculiar hum: not only history, but the frantic rhythm of a runaway engine beating in Pia, the town’s most dedicated, if narrowly focused, newsletter editor. This year the Golden Sprocket awaited the Most Enthusiastic Volunteer, and Pia, spectacles perched like inquisitive dewdrops on her whiskered nose, surveyed the scene with an editor’s sharp gaze.

“Mara, my dear cousin!” she exclaimed, a little too loud. Antique teacups rattled. “You’ve arrived! Just in time to witness greatness, or at least my earnest efforts toward it!”

Mara, a badger of placid disposition and excellent digging skills, ambled in, shaking dust from brindled fur. She moved with the quiet grace of a shadow. “Hello, Pia. Looks busy. Ready to polish some brass until it gleams like a summer’s dawn, I assume?”

“Polishing brass is merely a component of enthusiasm, Mara.” Pia’s tail flicked like a startled fish. “Enthusiasm must be communicated. Visible. It must shimmer. And most importantly—” she leaned in, whiskers tickling Mara’s ear — “it must be award-worthy.”

She led Mara to a long table draped in a robin’s-egg cloth. Tiny tin whistles and paper streamers waited as if to play a jaunty tune. Upon it sat a magnificent, somewhat alarming arrangement of teacups, saucers, and a towering edifice of biscuits, each wearing a miniature edible flag. Floral china sat beside bold geometric patterns, like wild strawberries among ferns. The biscuit tower looked faintly judgmental.

“Isn’t it magnificent?” Pia breathed. “This is how you show gratitude. How you radiate volunteer spirit!”

Mara blinked. “It certainly radiates. Are those digestive biscuits wearing tiny berets?”

“The finest! Each one a conquered polishing challenge. The berets are a subtle nod to the artistry of volunteerism. Your task is to keep the biscuits topped up. And please, do try to look inspired.”

Pia flitted off to offer unsolicited advice to volunteers wrestling a stubborn steam whistle. Therefore a low murmur of concern rippled through the hall. Mr. Digby, a kindly old mole whose spectacles were perpetually smudged with earth, paced near the magnificent Iron Duchess. Polished brass reflected worried faces.

“Has anyone seen the starting lever for the Duchess’s whistle?” His voice held a faint tremor. “We can’t do the demonstration without it, and young Seisyll swore he put it right here…” He gestured toward a cluttered workbench.

Pia froze mid-flit. Otter ears perked. The starting lever would herald the grand finale — immense potential for a volunteer showcase. If the demonstration was cancelled, her chances at the Golden Sprocket would diminish faster than a dewdrop at noon.

“A crisis!” she hissed to Mara, who was calmly arranging biscuit-berets. “A true test of volunteer mettle! The heart of the morning is about to stop beating!”

But Mara was not panicking. Badger instincts, honed by quiet observation, were attuned to clues. While Pia wrung her paws, Mara’s keen nose twitched. An earthy scent, distinct from coal and oil: a squirrel’s secret hoard, mixed with dried leaves. She had noticed Seisyll, a somewhat flighty squirrel known for forgetfulness, nervously eyeing a small dusty alcove near the locomotive’s enormous iron wheels, bushy tail twitching like a conductor’s baton.

“Perhaps,” Mara said softly, cutting through Pia’s drama, “it is not so much a crisis as a misplaced item. Seisyll has a habit of securing things in unexpected places.”

Pia called to mobilise the troops and initiate a search pattern, at least a moderately enthusiastic one. Therefore Mara ignored the theatre and padded toward the alcove. The air was cooler, old wood and dried leaves, like a forgotten corner of forest floor. She peered into the shadows. There, tucked behind a stack of ancient leather-bound journals, lay the gleaming brass starting lever. It nestled among a small pile of acorns, arranged with surprising neatness, and a perfectly preserved dandelion, fluffy head intact. Seisyll had decided it was the safest place in the museum.

Mara nudged the lever out. It clinked softly against stone, more satisfying than any frantic shout.

Pia, who had been orchestrating a theatrical search party of bewildered hedgehogs, spotted Mara emerging. She rushed over, whiskers drooping slightly at the lever in her cousin’s paw. For a fleeting moment the Golden Sprocket warred with genuine relief.

“Mara! You found it! You wonderful creature!” She snatched the lever with an eagerness that nearly sent it flying again. “Where was it? A daring rescue from a villainous magpie? A hidden cache from a forgotten tunnel?”

Mara shrugged, a twinkle in kind eyes. “Seisyll was tidying up earlier. He likes to keep things safe. Put it somewhere he wouldn’t forget, he said. Must have been the acorns that threw him off. Or the dandelion bouquet.”

The Iron Duchess let out a triumphant blast of steam, a mighty roar that shook the very foundations of the museum, signalling the start of its demonstration. Brass sang. Coal smoke sweetened. Pia stood a moment with the gleaming Golden Sprocket now firmly in her paw, awarded for Most Enthusiastic Volunteer. She looked at Mara, calmly wiping a smudge of dust from the lever with a paw that showed no hint of boastfulness, then at the happy upturned faces of the museum patrons.

She did not give the hall a speech about humble hearts. She looked at the over-decorated table, then at the engine that needed no berets to be grand.

“You know, Mara,” she said, the frantic edge gone, “that table was rather much. Like too many hats at once. Next time, hot tea, plentiful biscuits, and everyone welcome. And maybe let the steam engine do most of the shouting. Its voice is quite grand enough.”

Mara smiled, warm as a forest clearing. “A perfectly excellent plan, cousin.” The Duchess whistled again, and Pia left the biscuit flags where they were, slightly crooked, and did not straighten them.
characters: Pia (an otter town newsletter editor), Mara (the badger cousin)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing story for teens
